title: Lenses, Interference & Diffraction
summary: Because light is a wave, it interferes and diffracts. Young's double slit gives bright fringes at $d\sin\theta = m\lambda$ (spacing $y = m\lambda L/d$); a single slit gives minima at $a\sin\theta = m\lambda$; a diffraction grating sharpens the pattern with $d\sin\theta = m\lambda$. (University Physics Vol. 3, Ch. 2–4.)

interference.plain: Two waves overlapping to reinforce or cancel each other.
interference.in_class: Bright/dark fringes depend on the path difference between the waves.

diffraction.plain: Waves bending around edges or spreading after a narrow opening.
diffraction.in_class: Sets the fringe pattern from slits and gratings.

coherent.plain: Waves that keep a fixed phase relationship, so their pattern is stable.
coherent.in_class: Required for a steady interference pattern (e.g. laser light).

path difference.plain: The extra distance one wave travels compared to another.
path difference.in_class: $\Delta = d\sin\theta$; sets whether waves add or cancel.

constructive interference.plain: Waves lining up crest-to-crest to make a bright spot.
constructive interference.in_class: Path difference is a whole number of wavelengths: $d\sin\theta = m\lambda$.

destructive interference.plain: Waves lining up crest-to-trough to cancel into a dark spot.
destructive interference.in_class: Path difference is a half-integer of wavelengths.

double-slit.plain: Two narrow slits that make an interference pattern of bright and dark bands.
double-slit.in_class: Young's experiment: bright fringes at $d\sin\theta = m\lambda$.

diffraction grating.plain: Many closely spaced slits that split light into sharp, separated colors.
diffraction grating.in_class: $d\sin\theta = m\lambda$ with very small $d$ gives sharp maxima.

wavelength.plain: The distance between successive crests of a wave.
wavelength.in_class: Symbol $\lambda$; sets the fringe spacing in every formula here.

concept_sections.heading: Converging and diverging lenses
concept_sections.explanation: A converging (convex) lens bends parallel rays to a focus; a diverging (concave) lens spreads them so they seem to come from a focus behind it. Ray tracing — a ray through the center goes straight, a parallel ray bends through the focus — locates the image, consistent with $1/f = 1/d_o + 1/d_i$.

figure.caption: Converging lenses focus parallel light; diverging spread it.

concept_sections.heading: Young's double slit
concept_sections.explanation: Light through two close slits overlaps and interferes, making bright and dark bands. Bright fringes occur where the path difference is a whole number of wavelengths: $d\sin\theta = m\lambda$. On a screen a distance $L$ away, the bright fringes sit at $y = \dfrac{m\lambda L}{d}$ — proof that light is a wave.

figure.caption: Two slits interfere: bright fringes at $d\sin\theta = m\lambda$.

concept_sections.heading: Single-slit diffraction
concept_sections.explanation: Even one slit spreads light into a pattern, because waves from different parts of the slit interfere. The dark minima are at $a\sin\theta = m\lambda$ (with $m = 1, 2, \dots$), where $a$ is the slit width. Narrower slits spread light more.

figure.caption: A single slit spreads light into a diffraction pattern.

concept_sections.heading: Diffraction gratings
concept_sections.explanation: A grating has thousands of slits. The same condition $d\sin\theta = m\lambda$ holds, but with so many slits the bright lines become very sharp and separated. Different wavelengths appear at different angles, spreading light into a spectrum — how we measure the composition of light.

figure.caption: A grating's many slits give sharp maxima: $d\sin\theta = m\lambda$.

concept_sections.heading: Thin films and resolution
concept_sections.explanation: Interference also happens in thin films (soap bubbles, anti-reflective coatings), where reflections off the two surfaces combine. Diffraction also sets the ultimate limit on how finely any lens or telescope can resolve detail — smaller wavelengths and bigger apertures resolve more.

figure.caption: Thin films interfere; resolution is limited by diffraction.

real_world_examples.title: Colors on a CD or DVD
real_world_examples.scenario: A disc throws rainbow colors in the light.
real_world_examples.how_the_math_applies: The closely spaced tracks act as a reflection grating; $d\sin\theta = m\lambda$ sends each color to a different angle, splitting white light into a spectrum.

figure.caption: A CD's fine tracks act as a grating, splitting light into colors.

real_world_examples.title: Anti-reflective coating
real_world_examples.scenario: Camera and glasses lenses have a faint colored sheen.
real_world_examples.how_the_math_applies: A thin coating makes reflections off its two surfaces interfere destructively, cancelling glare for the targeted wavelength.

figure.caption: An anti-reflective coating cancels reflections by interference.

real_world_examples.title: Telescope resolution
real_world_examples.how_the_math_applies: Diffraction blurs points by an amount set by wavelength over aperture; a larger aperture $D$ shrinks the blur, resolving closer stars.

figure.caption: A telescope's aperture sets the smallest detail it can resolve.

problems.prompt: Double slit: $d = 0.10$ mm, $\lambda = 500$ nm, screen $L = 2.0$ m away. Find the distance to the first bright fringe ($m=1$).
problems.hint: Use $y = m\lambda L/d$; keep everything in meters.

problems.prompt: A grating has $500$ lines/mm. Find the slit spacing $d$.
problems.hint: Convert lines/mm to lines/m, then take the reciprocal.

problems.prompt: Single slit of width $a = 0.020$ mm, $\lambda = 500$ nm. Find the angle to the first minimum.
In a double-slit setup the first bright fringe is $1.0$ cm from center on a screen $2.0$ m away, with $d = 0.10$ mm. Find the wavelength.
A grating with $d = 2.0\times10^{-6}$ m is lit by $\lambda = 600$ nm. Find the angle of the second-order ($m=2$) bright line.
For the double slit of problem 1 ($d = 0.10$ mm, $\lambda = 500$ nm, $L = 2.0$ m), find the distance to the third bright fringe.
Find the fringe spacing $\Delta y$ for $\lambda = 600$ nm, $L = 1.5$ m, slit separation $d = 0.20$ mm.
problems.hint: Adjacent fringes are separated by $\lambda L/d$.

problems.prompt: A single slit produces its first minimum at $\theta = 2.0^\circ$ with $\lambda = 500$ nm. Find the slit width.
A grating with $d = 2.0\times10^{-6}$ m is lit by $\lambda = 600$ nm. What is the highest order $m$ that can appear?
problems.hint: Set $\sin\theta = 1$ in $d\sin\theta = m\lambda$ and round down.
